title: Can a tardigrade survive in space?
hook: In 2007, dried-out water bears spent 12 days in orbit, exposed to open space.
summary: Yes: in 2007, dehydrated tardigrades were exposed to open space in orbit on the FOTON-M3 mission and survived the vacuum, although the Sun’s ultraviolet radiation sharply cut their survival.
cardText: In 2007, about 3,000 dried-out tardigrades spent 12 days in orbit, exposed to open space. The vacuum did not bother them; the Sun’s radiation, though, sharply cut how many survived.

cardBlocks.text: Picture an animal that, when the water runs out, curls up and waits. That is the tardigrade, or water bear, a segmented animal so small that the largest species is only just over a millimetre long. Dried out, it enters anhydrobiosis: its body folds up, its metabolism nearly stops, and it can handle temperatures from -272 °C to 150 °C, ten years without water and plenty of radiation.

In September 2007, some 3,000 tardigrades spent 12 days in orbit on the European Space Agency’s FOTON-M3 mission, in an experiment called TARDIS, exposed to open space. The result: the vacuum, which dries things out to the extreme, was no problem. When the Sun’s ultraviolet radiation was added, survival dropped sharply. Even so, they became the first animals known to survive exposure to space.
Dried-out tardigrades survived the vacuum of space in 2007; what hurt them most was the Sun’s ultraviolet radiation.

deepDiveBlocks.text: As it dries, a tardigrade shrinks into folds that cut its surface area and slow water loss. It also makes several proteins that protect its cells, although the exact role of some of them during drying is still uncertain.

TARDIS, which tested two tardigrade species in open space, was not alone: FOTON-M3 carried three tardigrade projects in 2007. Another, TARSE, studied resistance to space effects, and RoTaRad examined how radiation, mainly cosmic radiation, affected survival and reproduction.

Before the tardigrades, ESA experiments had shown that lettuce seeds and lichens can survive space conditions, and that bacterial spores shaded from the Sun survive for years. That feeds an old question: could life travel between planets inside meteorites? Other ESA tests showed that in the outer layer of a rock, down to 2 cm, nothing survives entry through the atmosphere. The idea remains a hypothesis.

support.excerpt: Water bears, also known as tardigrades, are very small, segmented animals. The largest species is just over one millimetre in length.

claims.text: In anhydrobiosis, a tardigrade’s body shrinks and folds, and its metabolism drops to a very low level.

support.excerpt: In the anhydrobiotic state, the metabolic activity of tardigrades drops to a very low level
The changes are easiest to observe as a shrinkage of the body (forming numerous folds which reduce the body’s surface area), namely the adoption of the tun formation

claims.text: Tardigrades withstand temperatures from -272 °C to about 150 °C, up to ten years without water and high radiation.

support.excerpt: they can withstand temperatures ranging from -272 deg C to +150 deg C, they can be without water for a period of 10 years, and they are extremely resistant to radiation.
Water bears are also very resistant to extreme temperatures, and they can survive from −272.8 °C (Becquerel 1950) to about 150 °C

The next project involved in the mission of FOTON-M3 was TARDIS (Tardigrada In Space).

Tiny invertebrates are the first animals to withstand the vacuum and radiation of space.

The Tardigrade Resistance to Space Effects (TARSE) Project was the first one involved in the mission of FOTON-M3.
scientists examined effects on initial survival, long-term survival and fecundity of selected species of limno-terrestrial tardigrades in extreme stress conditions (mainly cosmic radiation)

claims.text: Earlier ESA experiments showed that lettuce seeds and lichens survive space, and bacterial spores shaded from the Sun survive for years.

support.excerpt: Over the past 10 years, other ESA experiments have shown that lettuce seeds and lichen were also able to survive exposure to space.
If shaded from direct sunlight, bacterial spores are also known to survive for many years under space conditions.

claims.text: These results relate to the open question of whether life could travel between planets inside meteorites.

support.excerpt: Could life as we know it have started elsewhere, to be carried later for instance on a meteorite and delivered here on Earth?
Only an organism that could live inside deeper cracks or pores in the rock could perhaps survive.
